title: Paradoxes in Generation Z's Media Consumption and Fake News Perception: An International Comparative Study (Paradoxos da Geração Z no Consumo de Média e na Perceção de Notícias Falsas: Um Estudo Comparativo Internacional)
screen_reason: Cross-national survey (N = 405 undergraduates in Spain, the United States and Portugal) that reports a share of respondents on a self-reported fake-news reception item (V7): 27.2% never, 33.1% rarely, 20% frequently or always. That is a RECALL (self-reported exposure) share of respondents above a threshold, which meets the RECALL inclusion criterion. Everything else in the paper is media-use description, perception-of-channel attribution, or scale means.

estimates.country: Espanha, Estados Unidos e Portugal (Spain, the United States and Portugal)
estimates.platform: online questionnaire (Google Forms); respondents report on their overall information consumption, not on a single platform
estimates.date: novembro de 2024 e maio de 2025 (November 2024 to May 2025)
estimates.measure_type: % of respondents who say they receive fake news 'frequently' or 'always'
estimates.value_raw: 20% ("apenas 20% referem receber frequentemente ou sempre notícias falsas" / "only 20% report receiving fake news frequently or always"); same item: 27.2% never, 33.1% rarely
estimates.denominator: 405 undergraduate university students from three countries (Spain N = 150, United States N = 151, Portugal N = 104), convenience sample
estimates.definition: Respondent selected 'Frequentemente' (frequently) or 'Sempre' (always) on item V7 'Receção de notícias falsas' (reception of fake news), a 1-5 frequency scale (1 = Nunca / never, 2 = Quase nunca / almost never, 3 = Ocasionalmente / occasionally, 4 = Frequentemente / frequently, 5 = Sempre / always). No definition of 'fake news' was supplied to respondents.
estimates.misinfo_def: No explicit definition is given; the questionnaire item asks only about 'notícias falsas' (fake news). Framing in the introduction: "as notícias falsas e a desinformação emergiram como um fenómeno massivo e grave, com impacto global" ("fake news and disinformation have emerged as a massive and serious phenomenon with global impact")
estimates.source_quote:
Importa salientar, a partir dos resultados fornecidos pela V7 (ver Tabela 1), que 27,2% dos
participantes afirmam nunca ter recebido notícias falsas, 33,1% declaram ter recebido rara-
mente, enquanto apenas 20% referem receber frequentemente ou sempre notícias falsas.
estimates.page_loc: Section 3.2 'Receção, Perceção e Gestão de Notícias Falsas Pelos Jovens', p. 12; item defined in Table 1, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Respondents' own judgement of how often they receive fake news; single self-report item (V7) on a 1-5 frequency scale, adapted from the European Commission 'Media Use in the European Union' (2019) and Digital News Report.es 2020 instruments. No external verification of what respondents counted as fake news, and no reliability statistics reported for the item.
estimates.moderator_quote: Foi utilizada uma amostra por conveniência (N = 405), para assegurar que os três países incluídos obtivessem um número suficiente de respostas. A descrição da amostra em cada país, considerando que todos os sujeitos eram estudantes universitários de licenciatura, foi a seguinte: Espanha (N = 150...); Estados Unidos (N = 151...); Portugal (N = 104...). [English: A convenience sample (N = 405) was used, to ensure that the three countries included obtained a sufficient number of responses. The description of the sample in each country, all subjects being undergraduate university students, was as follows: Spain (N = 150), United States (N = 151), Portugal (N = 104).]
estimates.notes: Value is pooled across the three countries; the paper reports NO country-level share for this item, only one-way ANOVA means on the 1-5 scale (Spain 2.45, United States 2.34, Portugal 2.51) with no significant country effect (F = 0.627, Sig. 0.535), so no country rows are created. Data collection spanned November 2024-May 2025; year coded 2025 as the closing year of the fielding window. Sample is undergraduate students (generation Z), a convenience sample the authors themselves flag as a limitation ('o estudo apresente como limitação principal o facto de se restringir a estudantes universitários'). QUOTE NOTE: the source_quote is copied exactly as the text file renders it, including the PDF's hyphenated line break in 'rara- mente' (raramente). English translation: 'It is worth noting, from the results provided by V7 (see Table 1), that 27.2% of participants state they have never received fake news, 33.1% declare they have rarely received it, while only 20% report receiving fake news frequently or always.'

missed_or_uncertain: Four families of numbers were seen and deliberately NOT extracted. (1) V10 'Na sua opinião, quais os canais que mais difundem notícias falsas?' (in your opinion, which channels most spread fake news?), Table 6 and p. 14, gives frequently+always shares for Facebook 78.3%, X 65.7%, TikTok 65.4%, word of mouth 61%, Instagram 58.5%, websites 57.3%, WhatsApp 52.6%, traditional media 27.2%. These are perceptions of WHICH CHANNEL spreads fake news, i.e. attribution of blame to a platform, not a report of what the respondent personally encountered or of the amount of misinformation in their own feed; treating 78.3% as a Facebook exposure estimate would be badly misleading. An adjudicator who applies a wider reading of 'perceived amount of misinformation in one's environment' could add these eight rows (per-country breakdowns are in Table 6). (2) V9 / Figure 5, the topics respondents associate with fake news (politics 81.3/74.2/67.3 by country, humour and rumours 68/51.7/52.9, etc.) - a perception of topic, no prevalence denominator. (3) V8, self-rated ability to distinguish fake news - discernment self-efficacy, explicitly excluded. (4) Externally cited figures in the introduction that must not be kept under R8: '69% da população da União Europeia é frequentemente exposta a notícias falsas ou deturpadas' (Iberifier 2024), 84% of Spaniards seeing false information as a problem for democracy, 70% of Portuguese worried about online disinformation, nine in ten US citizens occasionally encountering inaccurate news and 51% of US adults finding it hard to tell true from false (Wang & Haner, 2025). All are cited from other sources, not this study's data. Also noted: the complement of the 27.2% 'never' response (i.e. 72.8% receiving fake news at least rarely) is NOT extracted, because R8 forbids computed complements.

rob.design: Convenience sample of 405 undergraduate students (Spain 150, United States 151, Portugal 104), online Google Forms questionnaire fielded November 2024 - May 2025; instrument adapted from European Commission 'Media Use in the European Union' (2019) and Digital News Report.es 2020; 30 variables / 105 items collected, 10 variables / 31 items analysed; informed consent obtained; analysis in SPSS v.29 using descriptives, contingency tables, chi-square and one-way ANOVA. No sampling frame beyond convenience, no response rate, no scale reliability (alpha) or validity statistics, and no inter-coder procedure (self-report only).
